summary: Analyzes security threats against the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP), which carries QoS and subscriber configuration between a network access server and an access node such as a DSLAM. It then lists the security requirements the protocol should meet. It is informational.

eli5.summary: ANCP lets the main office tell a local broadband box how to treat each customer. This document asks what bad things an attacker could do to those messages and what protections are needed.

questions: what are the security threats to ancp
what is the access node control protocol
what security requirements does ancp need

subtitle: What an attacker could do to the messages between a broadband access node and its network access server, and what protection the protocol must offer.

tldr.problem: The Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) lets a Network Access Server configure and monitor access equipment such as a DSLAM, so tampering with it could disrupt or steal service for many subscribers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds a threat model, lists attacker goals, attack types and attack forms, applies them to the four ANCP use cases, and ends with a list of security requirements for the protocol.
tldr.outcome: The protocol MUST offer mutual authentication of the AN and NAS, authorization, replay protection, data-origin authentication and DoS robustness, and SHOULD offer confidentiality.

today: RFC 5713 is an Informational document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets out threats and requirements rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Scope and Goals
sections.content:
ANCP carries QoS-related, service-related and subscriber-related configuration and operations between a Network Access Server (NAS) and an Access Node (AN), for example a Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer (DSLAM). This RFC studies its security threats using the use cases from the ANCP framework document and the guidelines of RFC 3365.

It highlights three concerns: protecting message content against eavesdropping, modification, injection and replay; preventing impersonation of an ANCP node; and preventing denial-of-service attacks that exhaust state, processing or bandwidth. Policy negotiation and authentication at the AAA server are out of scope. Requirement words apply to the design of ANCP, not to its implementation or application.
sections.eli5: The box in the street obeys orders from the central office. This document is about making sure nobody can fake those orders, read them, or flood the line with junk.

sections.title: System Overview and Threat Model
sections.content:
The system has a NAS, an AAA server (which supplies authorization information and configuration parameters), an AN that terminates subscriber access loops, a Home Gateway (HGW), Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) behind it, and an aggregation network joining ANs to the NAS. The analysis focuses on ANCP traffic between the AN and the NAS, which may belong to two different administrative realms.

The normal flow is: the AN discovers the NAS, announces itself, they exchange capabilities, the NAS sends requests, the AN processes and answers them, and the AN sends status reports. Attackers may be off-path or on-path, and passive or active.

The threat model assumes five adversaries: an off-path one at the CPE or HGW, an off-path one on the Internet or a regional network, an on-path one between the AN and the NAS, and an on-path one that has taken control of the NAS or of the AN.
sections.eli5: Think of a postman (the network), a head office (NAS) and a local branch (AN). Trouble can come from someone listening along the road, someone shouting from outside, or someone who has taken over the office or the branch.

sections.title: Attacker Goals, Attack Types and Forms
sections.content:
Attackers may aim to disrupt individual customers, to disrupt a large fraction of customers or the network itself, or to gain profit, for example by replaying another privileged client's old packets to get a better QoS profile on their own DSL line.

Five attack types are listed: denial of service (including a peer that ignores requests so the sender keeps retransmitting and allocating state), integrity violation, downgrading to weaker security mechanisms, traffic analysis (for example learning whether a subscriber is at home from a line-up message), and management attacks against the AN configuration and its MIB module.

They can be carried out through message replay, faked message injection, message modification, man-in-the-middle and eavesdropping. The discovery protocol is called out as especially vulnerable to injection.
sections.eli5: Bad people might want to break things, steal a better service, or just snoop. They can copy old messages, make up new ones, change messages on the way, pretend to be someone else, or simply listen.

sections.title: Attacks Against ANCP Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the ANCP use cases. During session setup, peering and capability negotiation, on-path denial-of-service, truncation, modification, replay and downgrading are possible.

  • Dynamic access-loop attributes: forged or modified rate information can distort downstream shaping at the NAS, and eavesdropping reveals clients' connection state and harms privacy.
  • Access-loop configuration: replayed Configure Request messages can swamp the AN, and replayed or forged privileged profiles can give an attacker's own DSL line better service or downgrade a privileged client.
  • Remote connectivity test: truncated or modified triggers and Subscriber Response messages can make tests fail or keep the NAS allocating state.
  • Multicast: replay or tampering can deny or reduce access to streams, interfere with accounting, or let the HGW or CPE trigger heavy ANCP activity with repeated join and leave requests.
sections.eli5: Each job the branch does for the head office can be messed with in its own way: faking speeds, stealing a better plan, spoiling a line test, or making channel requests pile up.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
From the threats, the RFC derives requirements for the protocol solution. It MUST offer authentication of the AN to the NAS and of the NAS to the AN, allow authorization at both, offer replay protection, and provide data-origin authentication. It MUST be robust against denial-of-service attacks, including a specific mechanism for the load a user could create by sending many IGMP messages.

It SHOULD offer confidentiality protection, SHOULD keep the number of AN/NAS interactions low in default configuration, and SHOULD ensure access control of management objects and possibly encrypt their values in transit. The RFC's own Security Considerations section only restates that the document is about threats and requirements.
sections.eli5: The rules say both sides must prove who they are, old messages must not work twice, the system must survive floods, and secrets should ideally be hidden too.
